title: Satellite Imagery Exposes Iran's Tactical Blueprint Against U.S. Bases in Middle East
snippet: Analysis of satellite imagery reveals Iranian forces systematically targeted early-warning radars before launching massive drone and missile attacks on U.S. installations, causing billions in damage.
content:
WASHINGTON — A detailed analysis of satellite imagery and briefings from regional security officials reveal that Iran executed a calculated strategy against U.S. military installations across the Middle East, targeting critical early-warning radar defenses before unleashing barrage strikes on aircraft, troop housing, and support infrastructure.

The offensive, which encompassed over 115 drone and missile attacks through August, damaged or destroyed structures at 26 military sites housing American forces and equipment. The resulting damage has cost billions of dollars and forced a significant realignment of the American posture in the region, including the tactical relocation of key defense systems and aircraft out of the Persian Gulf.

Blinding the Air Defenses First

According to technical intelligence experts and satellite data, Iranian forces opened the campaign by systematically attacking high-value radar arrays meant to detect incoming threats. Within the first 48 hours of the conflict in late February, strikes targeted primary defense radar domes at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait and Naval Support Activity Bahrain. Mobile radar units in Saudi Arabia and Jordan were also hit early on.

Among the hardest-hit defense assets was a specialized Army early-warning radar system in Jordan—one of only 13 operated by the U.S. globally, valued at roughly $500 million. A separate $1.1 billion long-range defense radar system in Qatar sustained extensive damage during the strikes.

“Targeting these specialized radar assets was clearly designed to degrade the immediate countermeasure capabilities of U.S. and allied forces,” noted N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services. “By crippling early-warning systems, subsequent waves of strikes faced far less opposition.”

Widespread Destruction Across Regional Hubs

Once regional detection networks were compromised, Iranian strikes expanded to hit maintenance facilities, supply warehouses, and troop living quarters across Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. In Kuwait alone, Ali Al Salem Air Base endured at least 30 strikes, destroying over a dozen aircraft hangars and damaging nearby facilities.

At Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, attacks severely damaged a Boeing E-3 Sentry surveillance aircraft, two aerial refueling tankers, and several support buildings. In total, congressional reports confirm at least 15 U.S. aircraft sustained damage during the offensive.

Military analysts warn that the vulnerability of fixed installations to relatively low-cost drone salvos marks a fundamental shift in modern warcraft. “This should be a wake-up call for the United States,” said Raphael Cohen, director of the National Security Program at the RAND School of Public Policy. “The era of relying on permanent, fixed infrastructure in the Middle East as we did for decades is over.”

Pentagon Maintains Forces Are Resilient

Despite visual evidence showing extensive base damage and structural losses, U.S. Central Command has routinely declined to elaborate on specific equipment casualties, citing operational security. Meanwhile, public satellite imagery providers faced temporary restrictions from U.S. officials during the early months of the conflict, delaying full visual confirmation of strike severity until recent months.

Addressing the fallout, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell stated that U.S. installations remain secure. “Our forces and bases are well protected and America’s military is stronger than ever,” Parnell said, emphasizing that service members retain all necessary resources to execute their mission in the region.
